synopsis: A machine may operate across 100 or more job sites and applications, with different geometry, surfaces, traffic and light; the braking system must work across site types, weather, lighting and machine models [f16, f276, f2956]. Site controls materially affect the same braking algorithm’s safety results, and machinery conformity and functional-safety verification do not guarantee mine authorisation; destination-site legislation and site acceptance therefore remain essential [f804, f2930, f2271, f806]. The accident evidence underscores transport and pedestrian hazards: British quarry guidance attributes 40% of accidents and 60% of deaths to transport, while vehicle or machine strikes were the leading cause of death at US road construction sites during 2005–2016 [f11493, f3549, f11496]. Virtual coverage should include genuinely different captured environments, site-specific human behaviour, traffic rules and geometry, but no standard specifying the number of exact sites needed for broad coverage was found, and road-oriented tools require adaptation [f4106, f4355, f10670, f4320, f8337, f8607]. Confidence remains constrained by missing public off-road exposure data and uncertain transfer of on-road rare-event acceleration; the proposed response to field-engineer objections is field-derived parameter distributions and shadow-mode fleet collection through mid-2027 [f6918, f1114, f7440, f10659, f10669, f10650].
